newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Oil no inflation worry but Europe beware.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Oil no inflation worry but Europe beware.

text.p: By Jacqueline Thorpe,
Oil prices have retreated off heady mid-October highs and analysts say only a new, prolonged rise would pose a serious threat to inflation around the world.
Nevertheless, economists are keeping a wary eye on crude.
While oil prices around their recent highs of $25 per barrel throughout 1997 would certainly stoke inflation, the impact would not be alarming.
But even the smallest bump up could present a policy nightmare in Europe, where governments are furiously trying to curb spending and cut deficits to prepare for monetary union.
"It is a risk rather than a forecast," said Ian McCafferty, director of international economics at NatWest Capital Markets in London.

"But in Europe, it provides one of the major risks that all of the script in the run-up to the Maastricht Treaty could go wrong," he said. "If we get an external shock that both depresses GDP and raises inflation, it poses quite a big policy dilemma for the authorities, particularly the Bundesbank."
OIL PRICES GEAR BACK

Low heating oil stocks in the run-up to winter helped feed a scorching rally in crude, sending the price up 40 percent in four months to a six-year peak of $25.06 per barrel. The increase put prices $9 above levels a year ago.
So far, though, crude prices appear to have stabilised. Benchmark Brent crude was quoted in Europe at $23.04 in the early afternoon on Wednesday.

"We are unlikely to see prices averaging next year where they are currently, so they are likely to recede slightly over the next several monthsas as a bullish influence in the commodity market and the economic situation as whole," said Leslie Nicholas, commodity analyst at GNI Ltd. in London.
Two main factors were likely to encourage oil prices lower, Nicholas said.
First, in the United States the government has moved to squelch the rise in heating oil prices.

"They've encouraged refiners informally to increase their output of heating oil for the winter to try to avoid these spikes in the domestic market and the knock-on effect on the world price of crude," he said.

Second, the anticipated return to Iraqi oil on to world markets would put pressure on prices. An oil-for-food deal between Iraq and the United Nations has been stalled since last May but, with the U.S. elections out of the way, analysts expect renewed attempts to break the log-jam.
RISE MUST BE SUSTAINED TO PRESSURE INFLATION
Nevertheless, oil prices are significantly higher than last year and this is beginning to show up in input prices.
In Britain, for example, the crude oil component of input prices was up a hefty 31.8 percent year-on-year in September.
But analysts say prices must stay high for a sustained period to have an impact on inflation. Volatile swings can move underlying economic data either way.
While rising prices were bumping up British input prices, a 2.2 percent fall in imported crude oil helped keep the lid on South African producer price inflation in September.
The fall contributed to a low 0.1 month-on-month increase in the cost of imported goods, official statistics showed.

"It's not like an increase in wage costs that tends to be permanent at least for one year or two," said Ian Gunner, international economist at Chase in London. "An oil price rise can reverse quite quickly. It's always difficult to get bearish on inflation because of higher oil prices," he said.
Gunner said the impact of an oil price rise on inflation also depends to a large extent at what point in the economic cycle it appears.
"In the current environment where there's a lot of competition and growth is still fairly modest on a global basis, it is very difficult to pass on the increases," he said.
WHAT IF...?
McCafferty at NatWest said assuming a "normal winter" a return to a more sustainable $20 per barrel of crude was likely.

But even if prices did climb back to $25 per barrel, most major economies could swallow the rise without sliding into recession or seeing too big a boost to inflation, according to a recent simulation by NatWest.

Oil at $25 per barrel instead of $20 would push up inflation in the United States to 4.0 percent from 3.1 percent, in Japan to 3.9 percent from 2.3 percent, in Germany to 3.2 percent from 2.0 percent and in Britain to 4.2 percent from 2.8 percent.
"Inflation is, as one would expect, higher, but the outlook is not too alarming, with annual rates rising by no more than around 150 basis points relative to the base case," he said.
McCafferty said at the moment one would expect the impact of an oil price rise in the United States to be greater than in Japan or Europe because of tight labour markets and a closed output gap.
But U.S. labour markets are more sensitive to economic growth and demand than to prevailing inflation rates. With growth gearing down, oil price rises could be offset by declining wages.
In historical terms, a $5 or $9 rise in oil pales in comparison to the oil price shocks of the 1970s when prices more than doubled and inflation soared, he added.
However, a one percentage point rise in inflation in Europe could throw a spanner in the whole process of European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), McCafferty said.

Under the Maastricht Treaty, governments must bring their deficits down to 3.0 percent of GDP by 1997 to qualify for EMU in 1999. There is no designated level for inflation, although the treaty requires that each country be within 1.5 percentage points of the three best performers.

"If we were to see European central banks responding to that rise (in inflation) by pushing up short (term interest) rates by 50 to 100 basis points next year, that would depress growth even further," McCafferty said.
"We would fall below the minimum growth rate required to have any shot of reaching the Maastricht Treaty requirement.
"Any persistance of the current oil price would therefore have a much more insidious and damaging impact on the economies and the financial markets of Europe than initially it might appear," he said.
